questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The fire risk of an unprotected metal frame
questions.learningObjective: explain why an unprotected metal frame carries a serious fire risk
questions.stem: A dispatcher's log notes that a workshop's roof trusses are bare structural steel with no protective coating at all.

options.text: The frame can heat quickly and lose strength, so a small fire can bring the roof down
The frame is safe because steel does not burn, whatever else may catch around it
options.misconception: believes non-combustible steel makes the whole frame safe

options.text: The frame needs no protection because heat alone cannot weaken a structural member
options.misconception: assumes heat cannot reduce the strength of steel

options.text: The frame is safe because it is inside a building that is otherwise fireproof
options.misconception: relies on the fireproofness of other parts of the building

questions.explanation: Steel does not burn, but it heats quickly and loses strength as it does, so an unprotected frame can fail early in a fire. Whether the building around it burns matters less than how fast the frame softens.
questions.hint: Non-combustible does not mean strong when hot.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: An encased frame read after a fire
questions.learningObjective: read a burnt structure for the type of frame it had
questions.stem: A log entry describes a burnt-out building whose internal frame shows blistered paint, sagging beams and one side of the skeleton drawn out of shape.

options.text: The structure was a timber frame, and the shape came from burning of the joists
options.misconception: reads metal deformation as evidence of a timber frame

options.text: The structure was a metal frame, and heat plus water or impact distorted the members
The structure was a masonry shell, and the sagging shows the walls had collapsed
options.misconception: treats a metal skeleton as a collapsed masonry shell

options.text: The structure cannot be identified, because fire leaves no readable structural traces
options.misconception: claims fire erases all evidence of the structure

questions.explanation: Blistered paint, sagging and drawn-out metal are the characteristic signs of a steel frame heated and then cooled or struck. A timber or masonry shell would leave very different traces in the wreckage.
questions.hint: Read the metal, not the general ruin.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A tall building's wall as a hung skin
questions.learningObjective: explain why the wall of a tall building can be understood as a hung skin
questions.stem: A dispatcher asks the engineer to explain in writing why the wall of a very tall building can be understood as a skin hung on a frame.

answer.exemplar: In a tall building the frame carries all the weight, so the walls are no longer load-bearing walls in the old sense; they are panels fixed to the outside of the columns and floors. Because the panel does not hold the building up, it can be made thinner and of lighter material than a load-bearing wall of the same height. The result behaves like a skin stretched over a skeleton, which is why such a wall can be opened up with long areas of glass.

questions.explanation: Once the frame carries the loads, the wall only needs to enclose the building and carry itself, so it can be thin and light. That is what makes the wall behave like a skin rather than a mass.
questions.hint: Ask what carries the load in a tall building.

questions.learningObjective: calculate the share of dead load carried by a steel frame
questions.stem: The log records a steel frame of 1200 tonnes within a total dead load of 2000 tonnes for the whole structure.
questions.explanation: The steel is 1200 of the 2000 tonnes of dead load, so it accounts for 0.6 of the total. That heavy share is why the material choice governs what height can be reached.
questions.hint: Divide the steel mass by the total dead load.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a civic building claims by its scale
questions.learningObjective: interpret the claim a civic building makes through its scale

stimulus.body: The dispatcher's log for a civic building records a portico of forty-five metres rising above the houses either side of the square, each of which is about nine metres to its eaves. The entry notes the log was kept by the clerk who booked the site.

questions.stem: From the dispatcher's log above, what does the portico's height claim about the building?

options.text: The portico matches the height of the houses so that the square looks uniform
options.misconception: reads the height difference as an attempt at uniformity

options.text: The portico was built tall so that the clerk could see the square from the steps
options.misconception: gives the portico a practical reason rather than a civic claim

options.text: The portico announces the building's authority by standing far above the ordinary city
The portico's height reflects only the available stock of stone in the region
options.misconception: explains scale by material supply rather than by intent

questions.explanation: A civic building claims authority by dwarfing the ordinary fabric of the city around it, and the log records exactly that contrast. Scale is a statement about status, and the clerk's note confirms the building's official role.
questions.hint: Compare the portico with the houses beside it.

questions.topic: A survey of a planned capital

options.misconception: calls the planned capital a copy of an older suburb

options.text: The plan is an old trading town whose streets happened to align with the river
options.misconception: reads a designed layout as an accidental growth

options.text: The plan is a military camp whose grid the survey mistook for a town plan
options.misconception: misreads a survey of a camp as a city plan

options.text: The plan is a planned capital, ordered from a single design rather than grown gradually

questions.explanation: A grid, a central square and radiating avenues in a single scheme are the marks of a planned capital laid out at once. An old trading town grows irregularly along its trades and river, not to a drawn plan.

questions.topic: What a continuous street frontage does
questions.learningObjective: explain what a continuous street frontage does to a street
questions.stem: A question asks what happens to a street when its buildings form one continuous frontage along the whole block.

options.text: The street becomes more open, because a joined frontage removes the sense of depth
options.misconception: believes continuity opens the street rather than enclosing it

options.text: The street becomes a room-like enclosure, and the traffic inside it is less visible
The street gains a clear middle, since the joined frontage pushes activity to the centre
options.misconception: believes a continuous frontage pushes activity into the roadway

options.text: The street stays unchanged, because frontage continuity only affects the buildings
options.misconception: believes the street is unaffected by how its edges are built

questions.explanation: A continuous frontage closes the view down the street and makes it read as an outdoor room. Because the enclosure is continuous, people within it are harder for drivers to see, which is why such streets need care.
questions.hint: Think of the street as a room with walls.

questions.topic: What a frontage rule produces
questions.learningObjective: interpret what a frontage rule does to the street wall
questions.stem: A log entry records that a regulation limits unbroken shopfronts on any street to twelve metres before a break is required.

options.text: The rule sets the minimum height of any building frontage in the district
options.misconception: reads a length limit as a height rule

options.text: The rule guarantees that every street will look the same along its whole length
options.misconception: believes a maximum length produces uniform appearance

options.text: The rule prevents long continuous runs of frontage and forces breaks in the wall
The rule stops shops opening at all in the streets where it applies
options.misconception: misreads a length limit as a ban on shops

questions.explanation: A maximum unbroken run forces a break, so the rule works on the length of continuous frontage rather than on appearance or height. It can still be read as a rule about how the street is allowed to close up.
questions.hint: Ask what the rule caps and what it forces.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The fire risk of an unprotected metal frame
questions.learningObjective: weigh two options for protecting a frame against fire
questions.stem: A dispatcher weighs two options for a goods shed: bare steel trusses, or the same trusses with a sprayed fire protection.

options.text: Spray the trusses, but only so that the paint finish lasts longer
options.misconception: gives fire protection a cosmetic purpose

options.text: Leave them bare, because steel will not burn and needs no protection
options.misconception: believes non-combustibility alone removes the fire risk

options.text: Leave them bare, but add sprinklers, which make the frame's condition irrelevant
options.misconception: treats sprinklers as making frame strength beside the point

options.text: Spray the trusses, because an unprotected frame loses strength sooner in a fire

questions.explanation: Bare steel can reach a critical temperature quickly, and once it does the roof can come down on the fire below. Spraying buys time by insulating the metal, and sprinklers work on the fire rather than the frame.
questions.hint: Ask how quickly the bare metal loses strength.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: An encased frame read after a fire
questions.learningObjective: explain how a fire-damaged frame is read for its history
questions.stem: A dispatcher asks the engineer to explain in writing how an encased frame is read after a fire that has gutted the building.

answer.exemplar: Even when the contents have burned away, the frame keeps a record. Steel that was protected by a sprayed coating shows the coating still adhering in patches, with the bare metal beneath blackened but sound, which tells the reader that the protection held until late in the fire. Steel that was left bare shows blistered, scaled paint, sagging beams and twisting columns, because the unprotected metal reached its critical temperature early. The state of the coating and of the metal therefore indicates how the frame behaved during the fire.

questions.explanation: The frame's own surfaces record the fire: protected steel keeps its coating and stays straighter, while bare steel blisters, sags and twists. Reading those differences dates the failure within the fire.
questions.hint: Read the coating and the shape of the metal.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The material that made height possible
questions.learningObjective: identify the material that made height possible
questions.stem: A dispatcher's log asks what made it possible for buildings of twenty storeys and more to be raised in the later nineteenth century.

options.text: Thicker load-bearing walls, which let masons reach any height given time
options.misconception: believes masonry walls can be taken to any height as built

options.text: A metal frame of high tensile strength, which could be built tall and slender
Lighter mortar, which reduced the weight of each storey so the walls could rise
options.misconception: credits mortar rather than the frame for reaching great heights

options.text: Wider foundations, which allowed a heavier building to be raised on a smaller plot
options.misconception: credits foundations rather than the frame for the greater height

questions.explanation: Height became possible because the load was carried by a frame with a high strength-to-weight ratio rather than by thicker walls. The other three changes help a building but none of them removes the wall's role as the load path.
questions.hint: Ask what changed in the load path, not in the details.

questions.explanation: Scale on a public square is a claim of precedence. By taking a whole side and rising above the fabric around it, the building states that the institution in it outranks the ordinary city.

questions.topic: What a continuous street frontage does
questions.learningObjective: interpret what a continuous street frontage does for the people who use it

stimulus.body: The dispatcher's log for a street describes buildings running in an unbroken line along both sides from the river to the market, with no yards, no side gates and no gaps of any kind, and it notes that the street is lit at intervals from lamps set against the building line.

questions.stem: From the log above, what kind of space does the street's unbroken frontage make?

options.text: An open avenue, because the continuous frontage removes the sense of enclosure
options.misconception: believes a joined frontage opens the street rather than closing it

options.text: An enclosed outdoor room, comfortable to walk in but hard to cross from the edge
A route of heavy traffic, since the unbroken frontage pushes vehicles to the centre
options.misconception: claims the frontage arrangement dictates the traffic flow

options.text: A market street, since an unbroken line of shops is what markets require
options.misconception: infers a market use from the continuity of the frontage

questions.explanation: Unbroken frontages on both sides form a single wall along the street, which gives it the character of an outdoor room. It is sheltered and comfortable, but the enclosure hides people at the edges from drivers.
questions.hint: Ask what the two lines of buildings make of the street.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a frontage rule produces
questions.learningObjective: explain how a frontage rule shapes what gets built
questions.stem: A dispatcher asks for a written account of how a rule about street frontages shapes what gets built.

answer.exemplar: A frontage rule is a rule about the grain of a street rather than about appearance. By fixing a maximum unbroken run it decides where walls end and gaps begin, and therefore where people cross, where they slow down, and where light reaches the pavement. Once the gaps are set, the plots behind them follow, because a break in the frontage makes a plot that can be entered, used as a yard or built on again. What is built on the street is thus shaped by the rule before any style is chosen.

questions.explanation: The rule fixes where the street wall breaks, and those breaks decide crossings, light and access. Plot sizes follow the breaks, so the rule shapes building before style is ever discussed.
questions.hint: Ask what the rule decides before style is chosen.

questions.topic: The material that made height possible
questions.learningObjective: compare the wall thickness of framed and load-bearing construction
questions.stem: A log records two buildings of equal height: one with load-bearing masonry walls 1.2 metres thick and one with a frame whose walls are 0.3 metres thick.

options.text: The framed wall is a quarter as thick, because masonry walls are simply wasteful
options.misconception: explains the thinner wall by taste rather than by load path

options.text: The framed wall is a quarter as thick, and the frame is what carries the loads
The masonry wall is a quarter as thick, because thick walls are cheaper to build
options.misconception: reverses which building has the thicker wall

options.text: Both walls do the same structural work, so the difference is decorative
options.misconception: ignores the difference in the load each wall carries

questions.explanation: The masonry wall is 1.2 metres and the framed wall 0.3, so the framed wall is one quarter as thick. The reason is the load path: the frame carries the floors, so the wall only has to carry itself.
questions.hint: Compare the thicknesses, then ask why they differ.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a continuous street frontage does
questions.learningObjective: explain how a continuous street frontage changes the working of a street
questions.stem: A dispatcher asks for a written account of what a continuous street frontage does to the way a street works.

answer.exemplar: A continuous frontage turns a street into a room. Two unbroken walls of building give the street a defined edge, shelter it from wind, and direct movement along it rather than across it, because there is nowhere to turn into. The same enclosure has a cost: the walls hide people standing at the kerb from drivers, so a street that reads as generous to walkers can be hazardous for anyone crossing it. This is why the treatment of the pavement and the placement of crossings matter more on such streets.

questions.explanation: A continuous frontage gives the street a clear edge, shelter and movement along it, but the same walls hide people at the kerb from drivers. Comfort for walkers and difficulty in crossing follow from the same enclosure.
questions.hint: Ask what the walls do for walking and for crossing.

questions.explanation: With no protection and untreated timber nearby, the frame had a direct route from the fire and little delay before it began to heat. Steel's fire performance depends on how quickly that heating begins.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A survey of a planned capital
questions.learningObjective: explain how a planned capital's survey can be checked against its scheme
questions.stem: A dispatcher asks the clerk to explain in writing why a survey of a planned capital can be checked against the scheme that produced it.

answer.exemplar: A planned capital is laid out before the first brick is laid, so the drawing and the ground should correspond. The survey records where the avenues run, how wide they are, where the square sits and how the blocks were measured out, and each of those can be set against the original plan. Where a street is a metre wider than the plan or a block is turned slightly, the survey shows the point at which the built city stopped following the drawing, which is itself part of the record of how the scheme was carried out.

questions.explanation: Because the scheme was drawn first, the survey can be compared with the drawing to show both the plan and where the building departed from it. That makes the survey evidence of intention as well as of the built result.
questions.hint: Ask what the survey can be checked against.

questions.topic: What a continuous street frontage does

options.misconception: credits the frontage with an acoustic effect it does not have

options.text: Light and long views, since a continuous frontage keeps the street open
options.misconception: reverses the shelter that a closed street provides

options.text: Shelter from wind and a strong sense of enclosure along the whole length
Room to turn off the pavement, since the buildings stand back from the street
options.misconception: claims a continuous frontage sets the buildings back

questions.explanation: Two unbroken walls of buildings shelter the street and give it a defined, enclosed character. They also block light and views, which is why the two kinds of street feel so different under the same sky.
questions.hint: Ask what two unbroken walls do to wind and to light.

questions.topic: The fire risk of an unprotected metal frame
questions.learningObjective: judge the fire risk recorded for a warehouse with combustible stock

stimulus.body: The dispatcher's note records that a bonded warehouse stores paper in racks under a bare steel roof of four bays, that the racks stand against the outer wall, that a notice in the yard forbids smoking, and that the alarm call came from a night watchman on his round.

questions.stem: From the note above, how should the fire risk to this warehouse's roof be judged?

options.text: The risk is slight, because the notice forbids smoking and the watchman is present
options.misconception: treats a posted notice as an adequate control

options.text: The risk is serious, because the fuel sits directly against an unprotected frame
The risk is slight, because the racks stand clear of the frame's outer bays
options.misconception: reads the position of the racks as removing the risk

options.text: The risk cannot be judged, because the note does not record the frame's section
options.misconception: refuses the given evidence as insufficient

questions.explanation: The fuel is stored hard against an unprotected steel frame, and a posted notice is a weak control compared with that arrangement. Neither the watchman nor the racks' position removes the heat path to the frame.
questions.hint: Ask where the fuel sits in relation to the steel.

options.text: That it was shielded from the fire, since blistered paint implies no exposure
options.misconception: claims blistered paint proves the member was protected

options.text: That it was heated so severely that the coating and the metal both failed
options.misconception: reads surface damage as proof of structural failure

options.text: That it was heated enough to damage its coating but not enough to deform it
That it was coated in a material that failed at a low temperature
options.misconception: invents a coating defect the record does not mention

questions.explanation: Blistering and scaling show that the member's surface reached a temperature that ruined the coating, while the straightness of the metal shows it stayed within the limits of its strength. Both readings together date the exposure.
questions.hint: Ask what the coating shows and what the shape shows.

questions.learningObjective: explain what the foundations of a tall building must be sized for
questions.stem: A question asks what a tall building's foundations must be sized for when the walls no longer carry the floors.

options.text: For nothing in particular, since a frame needs no foundations at all
options.misconception: claims frames need no foundations

options.text: For the total weight of the building spread evenly along the whole base
options.misconception: keeps the foundation sizing for a load-bearing wall

options.text: For the wind loads on the exposed wall, which dominate every calculation
options.misconception: makes wind the governing load for a foundation

options.text: For the concentrated loads delivered by the frame columns rather than a spread wall

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a civic building claims by its scale
questions.learningObjective: explain how a civic building uses its frontage to make its claim
questions.stem: A dispatcher asks the clerk to explain in writing how a civic building uses its frontage to make its claim.

answer.exemplar: The frontage of a civic building is a claim made in public. Taking an entire side of a square shows that the institution claims the centre of public life rather than a corner of it, and the height of the building means the claim is legible from the far end of the square and from the surrounding streets. Nothing is said aloud, but the arrangement says that this business of the city is more important than the trade and housing that line the rest of the square.

questions.explanation: Occupying a whole side of a square claims the centre of public life, and height makes that claim visible from far off. The arrangement speaks about rank without any words being used.
questions.hint: Ask what taking a whole side of the square asserts.

options.misconception: ignores the width of the street in the total

options.text: Each block with its street measures 120 metres across the shorter dimension
Each block with its street measures 150 metres across the shorter dimension
options.misconception: adds the street width twice to the block

options.text: Each block with its street measures 210 metres across the shorter dimension
options.misconception: adds the street width to the longer side of the block

questions.explanation: The block's shorter side is 90 metres and the street between blocks adds 30 metres, so the measured width is 120 metres. Adding the street twice or using the longer side both give a different figure.
questions.hint: Add the street width to the block's shorter side.

options.misconception: believes a continuous frontage drives people into traffic

options.text: It shows them clearly to drivers, which makes crossings easy and safe
options.misconception: reverses the visibility effect of a continuous frontage

It has no effect on them, since only the traffic is affected by the street

options.text: The ruled district reads as a sequence of separate places with legible entrances

questions.topic: An encased frame read after a fire
questions.learningObjective: explain why charring depth on a protected member is evidence
questions.stem: A question asks why the depth of charring on a protected frame member matters when reading a fire.

options.text: Because the depth of charring sets the strength of the surviving metal
options.misconception: confuses a surface reading with the strength of the member

options.text: Because it shows how long the member was exposed before its protection failed
Because charring proves the member was shielded from the fire for most of it

questions.topic: A tall building's wall as a hung skin
questions.learningObjective: identify a hung wall from a record of its construction

stimulus.body: The dispatcher's log records that the wall of a tall building is made of panels hung on steel rails fixed to the floor edges, that each panel can be unbolted and replaced from a platform, and that the frame continues above the roof as a service tower carrying the lift machinery.

questions.stem: From the log above, what does the record show about the wall's structural role?

options.text: That the panels were fitted after the frame to stiffen it against wind
options.misconception: treats the cladding as part of the structural frame

options.text: That the wall is a load-bearing curtain strengthened by the rails behind it
options.misconception: describes a hung wall as a wall that carries the loads

options.text: That the wall is a skin hung on the frame and carries none of the building's load
That the panels are temporary, since they can be unbolted so easily
options.misconception: reads replaceability as a sign of temporary works

questions.explanation: Panels hung on rails that are unbolted and swapped from a platform show an enclosure that carries nothing itself. The service tower above the roof confirms that the frame, not the wall, carries on upward.

questions.topic: The material that made height possible
questions.learningObjective: explain a limitation that shaped early tall building frames
questions.stem: A log entry notes that an early tall building's frame was cast in wrought iron and had to be assembled from short pieces on site.

options.misconception: credits iron with a fire resistance it does not provide

options.text: The material could not carry the load and was soon replaced by weaker stock
options.misconception: confuses the joining difficulty with a lack of strength

options.misconception: reverses the reason the short lengths were a problem

options.text: The material could carry the load but could not be made in one long length

questions.explanation: Wrought iron was strong enough to frame a tall building, but it could not be produced in long members, so the frame had to be built up from many short pieces. That joining requirement shaped the structure of early tall buildings.

options.misconception: assumes steps can only be built on a slope

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A survey of a planned capital
questions.learningObjective: explain what a survey of a planned capital reveals that an old town does not
questions.stem: A dispatcher asks for a written account of what a survey of a planned capital reveals that a survey of an old town does not.

answer.exemplar: A survey of a planned capital records intentions, because the layout was decided on paper before the ground was built on. Its straight axes, its central square and its graded approaches show a single scheme imposed on the site, and the survey can be read back against the original plan. A survey of an old town records the opposite, since its irregular streets, its odd plot shapes and its mix of building dates are evidence of piecemeal growth, and no single design sits behind them.

questions.explanation: A planned capital can be read against the scheme that produced it, so its survey is a record of intention. An old town's irregularity records growth by many hands, so no single plan lies behind it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the layout was decided before building began.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a frontage rule produces
questions.learningObjective: explain why a frontage rule is written as a maximum length
questions.stem: A dispatcher asks for a written account of why a frontage rule is written as a maximum length rather than as a required gap.

answer.exemplar: A rule expressed as a required gap would have to name a particular distance, and every site would then be judged against that number whether or not it suited the street. A maximum length of unbroken frontage works on the run itself, so a wide opening satisfies it as readily as a narrow one, and the rule can be applied to any building type without redesigning it. What the rule produces is still the same: breaks in the street wall at intervals, and with them entrances that are legible and crossings that can be found.

questions.explanation: A maximum length works on the run itself, so it applies to any site and building type without naming a fixed distance. The breaks it produces, and the entrances and crossings that follow them, are the point of the rule.
questions.hint: Ask what the rule lets a designer choose for themselves.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The fire risk of an unprotected metal frame
questions.learningObjective: explain why an unprotected frame gives a fire almost no time limit
questions.stem: A dispatcher asks for a written account of why a building with an unprotected frame is said to have no time limit in a fire.

answer.exemplar: The limit on a fire in a framed building is set by the frame, because a frame that cannot carry its load stops holding the floors up, and once the floors fail the fire has a new route upwards. Unprotected steel heats quickly and loses most of its strength within minutes of the temperatures a real fire produces, so there is little time between the start of the fire and the collapse of the structure. Protection delays that loss of strength, which is why it is described as buying time rather than as improving the frame.

questions.explanation: The frame governs how far a fire can spread, and bare steel loses strength within minutes of reaching fire temperatures. Protection delays that loss, which is why it is described as buying time.
questions.hint: Ask what limits how far the fire can travel upward.

questions.topic: An encased frame read after a fire
questions.learningObjective: read the direction of fire damage through the building
questions.stem: A log records that after a fire the ground-floor beams were blackened but straight, the beams of the floor above were bowed, and the columns at the head of the stair were twisted.

options.text: The upper columns failed first and the fire worked downward to the lower floors
options.misconception: reverses the direction in which the fire spread

options.text: The fire was most severe on the ground floor, and the upper damage was smoke only
options.misconception: reverses the order of the damage in the building

options.text: The fire worked upward from the ground floor, and the metal failed higher in the building
The damage was caused by the collapse of floors onto the structure below
options.misconception: invents a collapse that the record does not mention

questions.explanation: Straight blackened beams show a member that was hot but within its limits, while bowed beams and twisted columns show members that failed. The failure rising through the building indicates a fire that worked upward from below.
questions.hint: Ask which members actually failed and where they are.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A tall building's wall as a hung skin
questions.learningObjective: explain what it means to call a tall building's wall a skin
questions.stem: A dispatcher asks for a written account of what it means to say a tall building's wall is a skin.

answer.exemplar: A skin is something stretched over and hung from a structure rather than forming it. In a tall building the columns and floors carry all the weight and resist the wind, and the walls are panels fixed to the outside of that frame, carrying only their own weight and the wind. Because the wall is not a load-bearing wall, it can be thin, light and largely glazed, and the word skin records exactly that: the enclosure has been freed from the job of supporting the building.

questions.explanation: Calling the wall a skin says it encloses without carrying the building's loads, which frees it to be thin and light. The frame, not the wall, is what holds the building up.
questions.hint: Ask whether the skin supports the building.

questions.hint: Ask what the spacing does to the span of each floor.

questions.topic: The fire risk of an unprotected metal frame
questions.learningObjective: explain why height alone does not protect a steel frame in a fire
questions.stem: A question asks why a workshop's steel columns can fail in a fire even though it is a low building of only two storeys.

options.misconception: invents a height restriction on the use of steel frames

options.text: Because the members near the seat of the fire reach a critical temperature quickly

options.text: Because the columns of a low building are always made of a weaker steel
options.misconception: invents a weaker steel for low buildings

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: An encased frame read after a fire
questions.learningObjective: explain how a fire-damaged frame keeps a record of the fire
questions.stem: A dispatcher asks the engineer to explain in writing how a fire-damaged frame can be read for its history.

answer.exemplar: A steel frame keeps two records of the fire that destroyed the building around it. Members that were protected by a coating tend to be straight but covered in the remains of that coating, which shows the protection held and the fire was held off them for a time. Members that were left bare are blistered, painted, bowed or twisted, and riveted joints have drawn apart, which shows they reached a temperature at which they could no longer carry their load. Comparing the two groups places the seat and the spread of the fire.

questions.explanation: Protected and unprotected steel leave different traces, so comparing them dates the failure within the fire and shows where it was hottest. The frame is the fire's own record of itself.
questions.hint: Compare coated members with bare ones.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A tall building's wall as a hung skin
questions.learningObjective: calculate the area of a single hung wall panel
questions.stem: A log records that the wall panels of a tall building are 1.5 metres wide and 2.5 metres tall.
questions.explanation: The area of one panel is 1.5 times 2.5, which is 3.75 square metres. Multiplying this by the number of panels gives the area of the hung skin.
questions.hint: Multiply the width by the height of a panel.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The material that made height possible
questions.learningObjective: explain why the frame rather than the total weight governs height
questions.stem: A question asks why the frame's strength, and not the total weight of the building, decides how high it can go.

options.text: Because weight stops mattering once a building is more than ten storeys high
options.misconception: puts an arbitrary storey count on the point

options.text: Because the total weight only matters for buildings of two storeys or fewer
options.misconception: reduces the importance of weight in low buildings

options.text: Because the frame carries the floors in bending and compression, so its members govern
Because the weight of the walls is excluded from the calculation of height
options.misconception: claims walls are left out of the load altogether

questions.explanation: Once the frame carries the floors, the governing check is the strength and stability of its members and their connections. Total weight still counts, but it no longer grows with height in the way a load-bearing wall's weight does.
questions.hint: Ask what the frame has to resist as the building rises.
